1.note: The pronoun **they** in this instance and in the rest of the verse likely refers to the Levites who were transporting the Box with accompanying music, as in 15:26. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And the Levites brought in the Box of God]

The author assumes that readers will understand that by **they brought in the Box**, he means that the Levites brought the Box into the City of David, as he describes in 15:29. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [And the Levites brought the Box of God into the City of David]
Here, the **face** of God represents his “presence.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in the presence of God]

2.note: The author assumes that readers will understand that he is referring to a **burnt offering** and to **peace offerings** that David offered personally on this occasion. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [his own burnt offering and peace offerings]
To bless people **in the name of Yahweh** was to name Yahweh as the one whom one hoped and believed would bless those people. Alternate translation: [and he called upon Yahweh to bless the people]

3.note: In each instance, the masculine term **man** has a generic sense that includes both men and women, as the context makes clear. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [to every person of Israel … to each person]
It might seem that including both of these expressions would be to express extra information in a way that would not be natural in your language. If so, you can omit the second expression.
The author is saying **every man of Israel** not to mean every single Israelite but those who were present. Alternate translation: [to every person who was present from throughout Israel]

4.note: Here, **to the face of** represents “in front of.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language, here and in verse 6. The UST models one way to do that.

4.q: וּ⁠לְ⁠הַזְכִּיר֙ וּ⁠לְ⁠הוֹד֣וֹת וּ⁠לְ⁠הַלֵּ֔ל לַ⁠יהוָ֖ה אֱלֹהֵ֥י יִשְׂרָאֵֽל
4.note: The author assumes that readers will understand that by **to make {one} remember**, he means that these Levites were to remind the Israelites, through their songs, of what Yahweh had done for them. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [to remind the Israelites what Yahweh, their God, had done for them and to thank and praise him for that]

5.note: See how you translated the term “seconds” in 15:18. Alternate translation: [his assistant]

7.note: It might seem that saying both **On that day** and **then** would be to express extra information in a way that would not be natural in your language. If so, you can omit the term “then.” Alternate translation: [On that day David appointed]

The author assumes that readers will understand that by **that day**, he means the day when the Israelites brought the Box to Jerusalem. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [On the day when the Israelites brought the Box to Jerusalem,]

The author is using **at the first** as a common expression of his culture to mean “initially” or “for the first time.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [appointed for the first time] or [initially appointed]

Here, **hand** represents the agency of a person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Asaph and his fellow Levites to be the ones to thank Yahweh]

In verses 8–36b, the author provides the words to a song that David apparently composed for this occasion and had Asaph and his fellow Levites sing. (Verse 36c tells how the Israelites responded afterwards.) In your translation, use a natural way of introducing this direct quotation of the words to this song. Alternate translation: [and his brothers, giving them this song to sing,]

8.note: See the discussion in the introduction to this chapter of how portions of this song constitute all or part of several psalms in the book of Psalms. If you have already translated those psalms, that will help you translate this song. See the chapter introduction for a list of what psalm passages correspond to which portions.

The implied “you” in the imperatives **Give thanks**, **call**, and **make known** is plural because David, through this song, is addressing all the Israelites who are present. So use the plural form in your translation if your language marks that distinction. The imperatives in the rest of the song are also plural.

David is using **call on his name** as a common expression of the culture to mean “acknowledge him as your God.” He means that the Israelites whom he is addressing should acknowledge Yahweh by name as their God. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [acknowledge him as your God]

10.note: David is using the possessive form to describe a **name** that is characterized by **holiness**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [in his holy name]

Here, Yahweh’s **name** represents Yahweh himself, who is holy. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [in Yahweh, who is holy]

David is using one part of a person, his **heart** (representing the location of his desires), to mean all of him in the act of rejoicing. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [let the people who seek Yahweh rejoice]

David is speaking of these people as if they were looking for Yahweh, as if he were a lost object. In this context, to seek Yahweh means generally to choose to know, worship, and obey him. Alternate translation: [those who worship Yahweh] or [those who are loyal to Yahweh]

11.note: The name **Yahweh** and the term **strength** together express a single idea. David is referring to **strength** that **Yahweh** provides. If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this meaning in a different way. Alternate translation: [Seek strength from Yahweh]

David is continuing to speak as if people should look for Yahweh. In this context, to **Seek** Yahweh means to depend on him. Alternate translation: [Depend on Yahweh for strength] or [Pray to Yahweh for strength]
Here, Yahweh’s **face** represents his presence. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [search for his presence]

David is continuing to speak as if people should look for Yahweh. In this context, to **search** for Yahweh’s presence means to endeavor to be in it. Alternate translation: [endeavor to be in his presence]

12.q: זִכְר֗וּ נִפְלְאֹתָי⁠ו֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר עָשָׂ֔ה מֹפְתָ֖י⁠ו וּ⁠מִשְׁפְּטֵי־פִֽי⁠הוּ זֶ֚רַע יִשְׂרָאֵ֣ל עַבְדּ֔⁠וֹ בְּנֵ֥י יַעֲקֹ֖ב בְּחִירָֽי⁠ו
12.note: If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine these verses into a verse bridge and move 16:13 before 16:12 in order to state who is being addressed before giving the content of the speech. Alternate translation: [Remember his wonderful doings]

Here Yahweh’s **mouth** represents what he has said. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and the judgments that he has spoken]

13.note: David is using the term **seed** to mean “descendants.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [descendants of Israel]
The pronoun **his** refers to Yahweh. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh’s servant]

David is speaking as if the people of Israel were the **sons** of Jacob. He means that they are his descendants. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [descendants of Jacob]
While the term **chosen** is a noun, it may be natural in some languages to specify an agent, as if this were a passive verbal form. Alternate translation: [whom he has chosen]

14.note: By using the possessive form **our God**, David is not saying that the Israelites possess or control Yahweh. Rather, he is using these words to indicate that Yahweh is the God whom the Israelites worship. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. The UST models one way to do that.

When David says that Yahweh’s judgments are **in** all of the earth, he means that they apply to all people everywhere on the earth. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [his laws apply to everyone on earth]

15.q: זִכְר֤וּ לְ⁠עוֹלָם֙ בְּרִית֔⁠וֹ דָּבָ֥ר צִוָּ֖ה לְ⁠אֶ֥לֶף דּֽוֹר
15.note: These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. You could combine the phrases and express the emphasis in another way. However, since Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it would be helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Decide as a team how you will approach pairs of phrases that mean basically the same thing. (You may already have done this if you have previously translated poetical or prophetic books.) Alternate translation: [Remember his covenant forever, yes, remember the word he commanded for a thousand generations]

In this context, the term **Remember** means to do more than recall information about something. David is using the term to mean “obey.” You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Obey the terms of his covenant]

David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [remember for a thousand generations the word he commanded ]

David is using the term **word** to represent what Yahweh said by using words. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the decree that he spoke]
David is saying **a thousand** as an overstatement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. The UST models one way to do that.

16.note: See how you translated the term “cut” in 11:3. Alternate translation: [he made]

David does not mean that the Israelites should remember two things, Yahweh’s “covenant” (verse 15) and this **oath**. David is speaking of this oath to represent that same covenant, which Yahweh confirmed to Isaac with an oath. Alternate translation: [and which he confirmed by an oath to Isaac]

17.q: וַ⁠יַּעֲמִידֶ֤⁠הָ לְ⁠יַעֲקֹב֙ לְ⁠חֹ֔ק לְ⁠יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל בְּרִ֥ית עוֹלָֽם
17.note: Recall how you have decided to translate poetic pairs of statements that mean basically the same thing. Alternate translation: [And he confirmed it to Jacob as a statute, indeed, he confirmed it to Israel as a covenant forever]
The pronoun **it** refers back to verse 15 to Yahweh’s covenant. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and he confirmed his covenant to Jacob as a statute]

In this context, the term **statute** does not refer to a law that the Israelites needed to keep. It describes a decree that Yahweh made that he would definitely carry out. Alternate translation: [as something that he would certainly do]

The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [he confirmed it to Israel as a covenant forever]

**Israel** and **Jacob** are two names for the same individual. So that readers do not misunderstand and think that “Israel” means the nation here, it may be helpful to use a pronoun that refers back to Jacob. Alternate translation: [to him]

18.q: לֵ⁠אמֹ֗ר לְ⁠ךָ֙ אֶתֵּ֣ן אֶֽרֶץ־כְּנָ֔עַן חֶ֖בֶל נַחֲלַתְ⁠כֶֽם בִּֽ⁠הְיֽוֹתְ⁠כֶם֙ מְתֵ֣י מִסְפָּ֔ר כִּ⁠מְעַ֖ט וְ⁠גָרִ֥ים בָּֽ⁠הּ
18.note:
If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine these verses into a verse bridge and move 16:19 before 16:18 in order to state under what conditions Yahweh said this before giving the content of the speech. Alternate translation: [when you were few in number,
according to a little, and sojourners in it, saying, “I will give to you the land of Canaan as the portion of your inheritance’]

18.q: לֵ⁠אמֹ֗ר לְ⁠ךָ֙ אֶתֵּ֣ן אֶֽרֶץ־כְּנָ֔עַן חֶ֖בֶל נַחֲלַתְ⁠כֶֽם
18.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [telling him that he would give him the land of Canaan as the portion of his inheritance]

The word **you** is plural because Yahweh was addressing Jacob individually. The word **your** is plural because Yahweh was referring to Jacob and his descendants. Use the appropriate singular and plural forms in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

Yahweh was speaking of the **land of Canaan** as if it were something that Jacob would inherit as his share of property from a relative who had died. He was doing that to represent the land as something that would always belong to Jacob and his descendants. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. The UST models one way to do that.

19.note: David is speaking as if the Israelites he is addressing through this song had actually been present at this time and been **few in number**. He is addressing them as representatives of their nation. Alternate translation: [when the people of your nation were] or [when your ancestors were]

David is using **according to a little** as a common expression of his culture to mean “very small.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [a tiny group] or [quite small]

The phrases **few in number** and **according to a little** mean basically the same thing. David is using the two phrases together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [only a small group of people]
The pronoun **it** refers back to “the land of Canaan” in the previous verse. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [in that land]

20.note: David is still speaking of the ancestors of the Israelites, but he is now doing so in the third person. (People writing poetry in Hebrew often shifted between persons in this way.) If it would be helpful to your readers, you could clarify how David is making this transition. Alternate translation: [And your ancestors wandered]

21.note: In this context, **a man** means **anyone**. Alternate translation: [anyone]

22.note: This is a direct quotation of Yahweh. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language. Alternate translation: [saying, ‘May you not touch my anointed {ones}, and may you not harm my prophets’]

If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [telling them not to touch his anointed and not harm to his prophets]

While Yahweh is using a verbal form that communicates what someone wishes another person would do, this is actually a strong command. If it would be clearer in your language, you could use a command form in your translation. The UST models one way to do that.
In this context, the term **touch** as the same meaning as **harm** in the next line. Alternate translation: [May you not harm] or [Do not harm]

The expression **anointed** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [the ones whom I have anointed]

Yahweh is speaking as if he had actually **anointed** all of the Israelites. He means that he has chosen them and set them apart for the special task of being his people, just as a person in this culture would be anointed when assuming an important position such as king or high priest. Alternate translation: [my chosen ones] or [the ones whom I have chosen]

23.note: Here, **all of the earth** represents all the people who live on the earth. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [all you people who live on the earth]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **salvation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [that he is the one who saves]

David is using **from day to day** as a common expression of his culture to mean “every day” or “continually.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [every day] or [continually]

24.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **glory**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [that he is glorious]

The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [recount his wonderful doings among all of the peoples]

25.note: The word translated as **For** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [Do this because]

The expression **is {to be} praised** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and everyone should praise him]

The expression **is {to be} feared** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and everyone should fear him]

26.note: Here the word **For** introduces not a reason but an explanation. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [After all,]

27.note: Here, Yahweh’s **face** represents his “presence”. Alternate translation: [Splendor and majesty are in his presence]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **Splendor** and **majesty**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [His presence is splendid and majestic]
Here, Yahweh’s **place** represents Yahweh himself. Alternate translation: [strength and joy characterize him]
If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **Strength** and **beauty**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [he is strong and joyful]

28.q: הָב֤וּ לַֽ⁠יהוָה֙ מִשְׁפְּח֣וֹת עַמִּ֔ים הָב֥וּ לַ⁠יהוָ֖ה כָּב֥וֹד וָ⁠עֹֽז
28.note: David is repeating the phrase **Ascribe to Yahweh** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat phrases for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [O you clans of the peoples, ascribe glory and strength to Yahweh]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **glory** and **strength**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [the fact that he is glorious and strong]

29.note: Here, Yahweh’s **name** represents his reputation. Alternate translation: [the glory of his reputation]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **glory**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the fact that he has a glorious reputation]
Here, Yahweh’s **face** represents his “presence”. Alternate translation: [into his presence] or [to his temple]
If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **splendor** and **holiness**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [because he is splendidly holy]

30.note: To **Tremble** was a symbolic action by which people showed reverent fear and awe in God’s holy presence. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [Tremble in reverent awe]

David is using **from his face** as a common expression of the culture to mean “because of” or “on account of.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [because of him] or [because he is so holy]

Here, **all of the earth** represents all the people who live on the earth. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [all you people who live on the earth]

The expression ** is established** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who has done this action, the context indicates that it is Yahweh. Alternate translation: [Yahweh has established the world]

The expression **it will not be shaken** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [nothing will shake it]

31.note: David is using **the heavens** to represent the beings who live in the heavens, and he is using **the earth** to represent the people who live on the earth. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Let the beings who live in the heavens rejoice, and let the people who live on the earth be glad]

David is using the two major components of creation, the **heavens** and the **earth**, to mean the entire creation. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Let every creature throughout all of creation rejoice]

If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [and let them declare among the nations that Yahweh reigns!]

Here David is using the pronoun **they** in a general sense, not to refer to specific people. Use an expression for this that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and let people say] or [and let it be said]

32.note: By **its fullness**, David means all of the creatures that fill the sea. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and all of the creatures that fill it]

David is not referring to a specific **field** or what is **in it**. He means fields and the things in them in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [let the fields and all that is in them rejoice]

David is speaking of fields and the things in them as if they were living things that could **rejoice**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [let it be as if the fields and everything in them are celebrating]

33.q: יְרַנְּנ֖וּ עֲצֵ֣י הַ⁠יָּ֑עַר מִ⁠לִּ⁠פְנֵ֣י יְהוָ֔ה כִּי־בָ֖א לִ⁠שְׁפּ֥וֹט אֶת־הָ⁠אָֽרֶץ
33.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [since he is coming to judge the earth, let the trees of the forest shout joyfully from the face of Yahweh]

David is speaking of **the trees of the forest** as if they were living things that could **shout joyfully**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [let it be as if the trees of the forest are shouting joyfully]

David is using **from the face of Yahweh** as a common expression of the culture to mean “because of Yahweh” or “on account of Yahweh.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [because of Yahweh] or [because of what Yahweh is going to do]
See how you translated the expression “the earth” in 16:30. Alternate translation: [text] Alternate translation: [the people who live on the earth]

34.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [Since Yahweh is good, give thanks to him]
Here the word **for** introduces not a reason but an explanation. Alternate translation: [indeed,]

35.q: וְ⁠אִמְר֕וּ הוֹשִׁיעֵ֨⁠נוּ֙ אֱלֹהֵ֣י יִשְׁעֵ֔⁠נוּ וְ⁠קַבְּצֵ֥⁠נוּ וְ⁠הַצִּילֵ֖⁠נוּ מִן־הַ⁠גּוֹיִ֑ם לְ⁠הֹדוֹת֙ לְ⁠שֵׁ֣ם קָדְשֶׁ֔⁠ךָ לְ⁠הִשְׁתַּבֵּ֖חַ בִּ⁠תְהִלָּתֶֽ⁠ךָ
35.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [And ask the God of your salvation to save you and gather you and deliver you from the nations so that you may give thanks to the name of his holiness and glorify yourselves in his praise]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **salvation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [God our Savior]

While, in many other parts of the Bible, the expression “gather us” means “bring us back from exile,” in this historical context it means “keep us together” or “make us unified.” Alternate translation: [and keep us together]

The expressions **to give thanks** and **to glory ourselves** express the goal or purpose of the request **gather us and deliver us from the nations**. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose. Alternate translation: [so that we may give thanks to the name of your holiness and glory ourselves in your praise]

David is using the possessive form to describe a **name** that is characterized by **holiness**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [to your holy name]
Here, Yahweh’s **name** represents his reputation. Alternate translation: [to you for your reputation for being holy]

The sense of this expression is not that the Israelites would glorify themselves but that they would praise Yahweh as the one they glorified. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [to praise you as the one whom we glorify]

36.note: The expression **Blessed be** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [May people bless Yahweh]

David is using **from everlasting and to everlasting** as a common expression of his culture to mean “for all eternity” or “forever.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [for all eternity] or [forever]

The term **Amen** is a Hebrew word that means “truly” or “may it be so.” The people of many Christian communities use this Hebrew word in their worship, and your readers may recognize it and understand its meaning. You will need to decide if you will present this word in its Hebrew form in your translation or if you will instead translate its meaning into your language. Both approaches have broad support. If you use the Hebrew word, you could spell it the way it sounds in your language and then put the translation in a footnote. Alternate translation: [Truly] or [May it be so]

37.note: The pronoun **he** refers to David. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And David left] or [And David stationed]
See how you translated the term “brothers” in 5:7. Alternate translation: [and his kinsmen] or [and his relatives]

Here, **to the face of** represents “in front of.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language, here and in verse 39. Alternate translation: [in front of … in front of]

The author is using **according to the matter of a day in its day** as a common expression of his culture to mean “as the duties of each day required.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [as the duties of each day required]

38.note: See the discussion in the introduction to this chapter of why the author may say **their brothers** rather than **his brothers** after one occurrence of that name. Alternate translation: [and Obed Edom and Jeiel and their brothers]

See the discussion in the introduction to this chapter of the possibility that this may be another man named **Obed Edom** different from the man described earlier in the verse. The UST models one way to acknowledge this possibility.

41.note: The expressions **chosen** and **were designated** are a passive verbal forms. If your language would not use those forms, you could express the ideas in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and the rest of the ones whom David chose, whom he designated]

This clause does not seem to state the reason why these Levites were to give **thanks to Yahweh**. Instead, it seems to be an example of what they were to sing in order to thank and praise Yahweh. This clause occurs in many of the psalms and in other biblical contexts, including here in verse 34. The ULT marks this as a quotation from the worship music of Israel by placing quotation marks at its beginning and end. You may be able to do the same or use some other punctuation or convention of your language to indicate that this is a quotation

42.note: The author is using the possessive form not to describe **music** that belonged to **God** but to describe **music** that was offered to praise **God**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. The UST models one way to do that.

43.note: The author is using **a man to his house** as a common expression of this culture to “each one to his own home.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [each one to his own home]
In this context, the term **house** refers to all the people living in a house, that is, a household. Alternate translation: [his household]
